Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Baldwin Creek Climbing Area | Wyoming View Map In Full Screen The Baldwin Creek Climbing Area has about 50 established rock climbs ranging in difficulty from 5.11 to 5.14. The average difficulty of these climbs exceeds those of two of the other popular rock-climbing areas near Lander-Sinks Canyon and Wild Iris. The rocks of interest to climbers make up the middle member of the Bighorn dolomite, a geologic formation of Ordovician age. The main body of the formation was deposited in a warm shallow sea between 470 and 450 million years ago. Dolomite is similar to limestone (calcium carbonate) but is much richer in magnesium. Factors influencing sedimentation were probably constant for a long time because the cliffs are very uniform in composition, texture and color. They have few cracks or other flaws, and as a result, they provide uniformly difficult rock climbing opportunities. pages.text: Bangladesh: Wage protests force hundreds of garment factories to close Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close 3 November 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Mukimul Ahsan , BBC Bangla and Koh Ewe Garment workers in Bangladesh stage protests to demand higher wages Hundreds of garment factories in Bangladesh have been forced to close after days-long protests by workers demanding higher wages. On Sunday, protests in the capital Dhaka turned violent with protesters blocking roads, vandalising factories and setting vehicles on fire. They also clashed with police, who fired tear gas to disperse them. Police later said that dozens of protesters had been arrested. Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242; £180), more than double the current standard, citing rising costs of living. Bangladesh's textile industry employs around four million workers and manufactures garments for major global brands including H&M, Primark and Uniqlo. There are fears in the industry that the prolonged unrest could disrupt production and affect international buyers, state news agency BSS reported. The garment industry generates nearly $40bn every year for Bangladesh, accounting for around 10% of its GDP. Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton stepped forward with a plan to establish a national bank—which still stands in Independence National Historical Park—that would give the federal government more authority to handle the fiscal situation. His proposal incited a debate that tested the US Constitution’s boundaries and laid the foundation for the country’s financial system. Since then, banking, lending money, and printing currency have continued to grow and fluctuate and entrepreneurial Americans, such as Maggie Walker , have led the banking world to new heights. Basic Energy Sciences The Basic Energy Sciences (BES) program supports basic scientific research to lay the foundations for new energy technologies and to advance DOE missions in energy, environment, and national security. BES research emphasizes discovery, design, and understanding of new materials and new chemical, biochemical, and geological processes. The ultimate goal is to better understand the physical world and harness nature to benefit people and society. Major technological innovations don’t just happen. They typically have their roots in basic research breakthroughs over a period of decades. The BES program supports basic research behind a broad range of energy technologies, spanning energy generation, conversion, transmission, storage, and use. Many major innovations can be traced back to basic research supported by BES over the past 40 years. These include, for example, LED lighting; efficient solar cells; better batteries; stronger, lighter materials for transportation, nuclear power plants, and national defense; and improved production processes for high-value chemicals. The BES program is one of the nation’s largest sponsors of research in the physical sciences. The program funds basic science at nearly 170 universities

Established by the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) on December 2, 1980, the preserve aims to protect a landscape that contains an invaluable record of flora and fauna, the history of human migration between Asia and North America and supports an ongoing tradition of subsistence culture. An opportunity to travel to a land visited by so few can provide solitude and beauty not often available in others parts of the country. The public cannot enter into the cave. Basic Information about Cleanups EPA conducts and supervises investigation and cleanup actions at sites where oil or hazardous chemicals have been or may be released into the environment. Cleanup activities take place at active and abandoned waste sites, federal facilities and properties, and where any storage tanks have leaked. EPA, other federal agencies, states or municipalities, or the company or party responsible for the contamination may perform cleanups. Cleanup can also include site reuse and redevelopment. EPA's Cleanup Programs There are several programs under which EPA and its partners conduct cleanup-related activities. EPA's programs are described below. The tag lines in the listing should generally help you figure out which programs are appropriate for specific situations. Emergency Response - when the danger from pollutants poses an immediate threat to human health or the environment Superfund Cleanup - for large, abandoned hazardous waste sites Federal Facilities Cleanup - for cleanups at facilities owned by the federal government (includes Superfund and RCRA sites) Brownfields Cleanup - for assessments and cleanups grants related to potentially usable properties Underground Storage Tank Cleanup - a state-delegated program

A wide stretch of soft sand is the perfect place for a walk, kite flying and other fun on the ocean shore. The beach is bordered by a shore pine forest and a steep headland. Open fires are prohibited during fire season (July 1 - Sept. 30) including campfires, charcoal fires, cooking fires, and warming fires. The campground also serves as an ideal base camp for exploring the Land of the Yankee Fork, rich in trails, interpretive sites, and striking mountain landscapes. pages.text: BBC launches educational show in Hausa for millions out of school in West Africa Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live BBC launches programme for children forced from school by bandits and poverty in West Africa 16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Madina Maishanu BBC Africa, Goronyo Ifiokabasi Ettang/BBC Hadiza left school at 13 to get married and now spends her time doing housework As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school. "Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says. One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village. "They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says. Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married. "It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains. Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home. Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced. pages.text: Be Among the First to Explore Cape Froward, a Patagonian National Park at the End of the World | National Geographic National Geographic Traveller (UK) content straight to your inbox — sign up for our newsletter here TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD Be Among the First to Explore Cape Froward, a Patagonian National Park at the End of the World At the southern tip of mainland South America, Chile's newest protected wilderness beckons adventurers. The subantarctic landscape of Cape Froward National Park overlooks the Strait of Magellan. Eduardo Hernández Astudillo By Alexandra Gillespie Published October 20, 2026 Take Route 9 south from Punta Arenas along the Strait of Magellan until the road ends, then hike until you reach a 33-foot metal cross. This marks Cape Froward , the southernmost point in mainland South America, in a remote region where the Indigenous Kawésqar people have paddled the coast for 7,000 years , forests shelter endangered Andean deer, and bogs bank carbon by the ton. In 2027, the area will become Cape Froward National Park , the 19th and southernmost national stop on Patagonia’s 1,700-mile Route of Parks , a project led by the conservation nonprofit Rewilding Chile . Because there are no roads here, you’ll discover its raw wilderness on foot or by boat. ( See all 25 of the destinations that made our list of the best places to visit in 2027. ) When to Go Visit during the Southern Hemisphere's warm season, roughly October through April. Plump, wriggling ant larvae and helpless eggs sit waiting to be devoured, while hundreds of thousands of ants stand at the ready to ward off predators and parasites. There’s just one catch for these beetles, revealed in a new study published in the journal Cell . If one leaves the ant colony, it’ll be dead in less than a day. From bacteria living inside insect guts to mycorrhizal fungi on plant roots, symbiotic organisms abound across the tree of life, says Joseph Parker , an evolutionary biologist at the California Institute of Technology and senior author of the study. In the 1960s and ’70s, a countercultural movement drew a new generation of pioneers to the West. Suddenly, ski bums, scofflaws, draft dodgers and hippie homesteaders were joining the miners and hardscrabble farmers of mountain towns like Crested Butte, Colorado. Looking for a way to navigate both the Pontiac-bedeviling potholes in town as well as the dirt roads leading into the mountains, a small crew of Crested Butte transplants began building handmade off-road-ready bikes. They used a hodgepodge of vintage parts, in particular from World War II-era Schwinn bicycles. The group called itself the Grubstake Gang (named after a favorite watering hole), and they rejoiced when their heavy cruisers, outfitted with fat tires, proved capable of handling the punishing unpaved roads into and out of town. In September 1976, 15 cyclists attempted a seemingly impossible feat: riding these “klunkers” over 12,700-foot Pearl Pass to Aspen. The next day, just two riders rolled into Aspen; the steep Colorado stones of the 38-mile road had destroyed all the other klunkers. Around the same time, a group of teenagers in California’s Marin County—they called themselves the Larkspur Canyon Gang —were tinkering and racing their own garage-built bikes down the steep roads of Mount Tamalpais , north of San Francisco. pages.text: Ben Franklin Wasn’t Serious When He Implied the Wild Turkey Would Be a ‘Respectable’ National Symbol … but He Wasn’t Wrong, Either Skip to main content The head of a male turkey is distinguished by the colorful dewlap and caruncles on its neck. Joanna Lentini The wild turkey is a noble beast: the muscular, bronze-sheened ancestor of the barnyard turkeys we eat today. While the two technically belong to the same species, the barnyard variety is relatively new on the scene. People began domesticating wild turkeys in what is now Mexico more than 2,000 years ago, selectively breeding them over generations to become fat and docile. Wild turkeys, meanwhile, have inhabited North America for a much longer time—hundreds of thousands of years. Hunters still eat them, of course, and appreciate the lean gaminess of the wild flesh. But for most of us, the bird is less about sustenance than about a glimpse of the true national temperament: resourceful and restless, by turns noble and idiotic—as liable to swagger into view as to bolt for the trees. This feathery American character has long invited comparison with another native bird. When the Continental Congress first chose the bald eagle for our fledgling nation’s heraldry, Benjamin Franklin wrote to his daughter in 1784 condemning it as “a bird of bad moral character,” given to stealing food from smaller birds rather than hunting for itself.
